## Leaving home around 27: what does a rental budget buy?

::::: {.two style="margin-top:24px"}

:::: {.middle}

::: {.huge .accent}
26.6
:::

### years · Luxembourg, 2025

Estimated age of leaving the parental home.

::: {.small}
Eurostat · Both sexes. The indicator estimates the age at which 50% no longer live with their parents; it does not average individually recorded departure dates.
:::

::::

:::: {.middle}

### The question we can explore

For someone seeking a place of their own, where would **€1,200 per month** cover a **45 m² rental scenario** — and how has that changed since 2010?

::: {.small}
Budget expressed in 2025 purchasing power. Budget and area are illustrative assumptions, not measured young-adult averages.
:::

::::

:::::

::: {.small .rule}
A national indicator, not a departure age for each commune. The rental scenario explores costs; it does not explain why people leave or stay.
:::

::: {.source}
[Eurostat · Estimated average age of young persons leaving the parental household, yth_demo_030](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/databrowser/view/yth_demo_030/default/table?lang=en). 2025: 26.6 years; 2024: 26.9. Dataset snapshot updated 16 April 2026.
:::

::: {.speaker-note}
Allow about one minute. Connect the opening person aged 27 to the 2025 national estimate of 26.6. Eurostat's official title uses estimated average age; its definition is the age at which 50% no longer live with their parents. This does not establish an individual departure date or why people leave. Transition directly to the rental map: where does an illustrative €1,200 budget for 45 m² fit? Hold purchasing power constant. The census bars remain in the appendix for background. Do not suggest the rental map estimates departure ages or establishes causation.
:::

Local evidence / Schifflange

:::::::::::::::::::::::

## Housing stock is not housing access

::: {.subtitle style="margin-top:18px"}
Schifflange: can existing social housing meet young adults’ needs?
:::

::::: {.schifflange-layout}

:::: {.stock-baseline}
### What we know

**246 social rental dwellings**

Recorded in 2022; published by LISER in 2023.

A historical stock count. It does not tell us how many homes become available or serve young adults.
::::

:::: {.stock-questions}
### What we need to establish

| Question | Evidence needed |
|:--|:--|
| **Availability** | Vacancies, turnover and waiting times |
| **Access** | Eligibility and barriers, including for non-applicants |
| **Suitability** | Rents, sizes and locations matched to young adults’ needs |
::::

:::::

::: {.stock-action}
### Proposed action · Match provision to need

Commission an updated stock-and-demand assessment, including young adults outside waiting lists, to identify which housing response merits development.
:::

::: {.source}
[LISER, Observatoire social de Schifflange (March 2023), Table 20, pp. 62–63](https://schifflange.lu/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Rapport-Observatoire-social-Schifflange-final-compressed.pdf#page=62). 2022 stock: 100 municipal · 100 Fonds du Logement · 46 other providers. Excludes GLS, emergency housing and assisted ownership. The assessment above is proposed, not an adopted measure.
:::


::: {.speaker-note}

Schifflange illustrates what local evidence adds to the rental scenario. The 246 dwellings are a dated baseline, not evidence of adequate provision or vacancies. Walk through availability, access and suitability. The report recommends examining dwelling types, location and demand; the proposed assessment here adds a focus on young adults, including non-applicants. Present the French action as a proposal, not an adopted measure or a finding that one intervention is already justified.

:::

## The working setup I propose

Gertler, Galiani and Romero (2018) examined **203 empirical papers across nine economics journals**. Only **14% were fully reproducible from raw data to tables and figures**.

| Failure mode | My proposed safeguard |
|:--|:--|
| Code will not run elsewhere | Docker image; dependencies pinned with renv or Nix |
| Results shift between runs | Fixed seeds and inputs; a targets DAG to manage reruns |
| Output does not match the exhibit | Pipeline-generated tables and figures consumed by Quarto |
| Definitions drift between years | Unit-tested, versioned indicator functions; a change log |
| Failures go unnoticed | CI on every commit: rebuild, test and flag failures |


::::: {.setup-footer}

::: {.source}
[Gertler, Galiani & Romero (2018), *How to make replication the norm*, Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-02108-9); [supplement, pp. 1–2](https://media.nature.com/original/magazine-assets/d41586-018-02108-9/gertler-et-al.-Comment-supplementary-information).
:::

## One pipeline, five products

One shared set of documented indicators can support different audiences. Each product still needs editorial work, accessibility checks and disclosure review.

| Proposed product | Audience | Purpose |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Indicator dashboard | Communal services | Look up and monitor |
| Four-page note | Collège échevinal | Support a decision |
| Thematic report | Council and researchers | Document evidence and methods |
| Restitution workshop | Services and elected members | Challenge and contextualise findings |
| Public map | Residents and media | Explain the evidence |


::: {.speaker-note}

10:15–11:15. Different users need different products; shared indicators do not remove editorial and confidentiality work.

:::

::: {.eyebrow}
Appendix / Methods and limitations
:::

## How to read the results

| Method or limitation | What it means for interpretation |
|:--|:--|
| **Illustrative rental scenario** | Commune mean €/m² × chosen area. Advertised, not contracted rents; no adjustment for dwelling quality or size. Small flats can have different €/m². |
| **Constant purchasing power** | Historical budget = 2025 budget × IPCN(year) / IPCN(2025). €1,200 becomes about €876 in 2010. No earnings adjustment; classify using unrounded values. The nominal toggle is a different comparison. |
| **Incomplete coverage** | This workbook withholds rates below 30 advertisements. In 2025, 34 of 100 communes have rates; hatching means unavailable, not no housing. Do not generalise this threshold to other Observatoire products. |
| **Matched geography and sample** | Predecessor rates are offer-weighted only when every component is observed. The baseline 29 → 11 result concerns 29 communes observed in both 2010 and 2025; listing composition can still change. |
| **Counts are not housing access** | Unweighted commune counts are not counts of people, homes or vacancies. No confidence intervals or quality-adjusted rent index. Deposits, charges, eligibility, transport and shared housing are not modelled. |
| **No departure or causal estimate** | Eurostat’s departure-age indicator is national; the census is a 2021 snapshot. Neither provides a municipal departure series. The map does not show that rents caused delayed departures. €1,200 and 45 m² are chosen assumptions, not measured young-adult means. |
| **Local action remains a proposal** | Schifflange’s 246 is a 2022 stock, excluding GLS, emergency housing and assisted ownership—not current vacancies or youth provision. A local study is needed before selecting an intervention. |

::: {.small}
The reproducibility study’s 86% includes missing materials; it does not mean 86% of conclusions were disproved. Engineering safeguards shown are proposed practices, not all implemented in this repository.
:::
